questions.q: In a try ... except ... else statement, when does the else block run?
options: Every time, straight after the except block
Only when the try block finishes without raising any exception
Only after an except block has handled an exception
Only when an exception is raised that no except clause matches
questions.explain: The else block is the no-error path: it runs only if the try block completes without raising anything. If an exception is raised, the matching except block runs and else is skipped.
why_wrong: else is skipped whenever an exception occurred; the block that runs every time is finally.
Handling an exception is the except block's job; else is skipped whenever an exception was raised.
An unmatched exception propagates out of the whole statement; else does not run then either.

That message appears only when the exception is NOT caught; here the except clause handles it.

questions.q: Which clause of a try statement runs at the end in every case, whether the try block raised an exception or not?
questions.explain: The finally clause always runs last: after a clean try, after a handled exception, and even when the try block executes return. That is why it is used for clean-up work such as closing a file.
why_wrong: raise is a statement that throws an exception; it is not a clause of the try statement.
else runs only when the try block raised no exception.
except runs only when a matching exception is raised.

questions.q: A student checks 4-digit PINs with the function below. Which input does it wrongly accept, returning True?
questions.explain: re.match anchors only at the START of the string; it does not require the match to reach the end. For '12345' the first four characters are digits, so a match object is returned and valid() gives True even though the PIN has 5 digits. Adding the end anchor to the pattern, as in r'\d{4}$', forces the match to reach the end of the string and would reject it.
why_wrong: re.match must match at position 0, and 'a' is not a digit, so this returns None and is correctly rejected.
The space breaks the digits after two of them, so \d{4} cannot match at the start and the input is rejected.
\d{4} needs four digits and there are only three, so this returns None and is rejected.

questions.q: A scraper collects email addresses from a line of page text with the code below. What does it print?
questions.code:
import re
text = 'Mail raj.k@lpu.com or amit@gmail.com'
print(re.findall(r'\w+@\w+\.com', text))
questions.explain: \w matches letters, digits and underscore only, not a dot. \w+ must run straight into @, so the match cannot include 'raj.', and findall starts the first match at 'k', giving 'k@lpu.com'. The second address fits completely. A class that allows a dot, such as [\w.]+@, would capture raj.k@lpu.com.
why_wrong: Assumes \w matches '.'. It does not, so 'raj.' cannot be part of the match.
Assumes the regex rejects the whole first address. findall finds the part of it that does fit, starting at 'k'.
Assumes findall stops after the first match, like search(). It returns every match.

questions.q: What does the code below print?
questions.code:
import re page = '

Hi

ok' print(re.findall(r'<(.*?)>', page))
questions.explain: .*? is lazy, so each match stops at the first > after its <, giving four separate tag matches. The pattern has one capturing group, so findall returns only the text inside the brackets for each match. The closing tags keep their slash, giving ['p', '/p', 'i', '/i'].
why_wrong: Ignores the group. With one capturing group, findall returns the group's text, not the whole match.
Assumes closing tags are skipped. .*? matches '/p' just as it matches 'p'.
Treats .*? as greedy .*, which would run from the first < to the last >.
